Senses.Note: Zen bends two ordinary looking verbs and an exclamation into the stable monastic name for Yunmen's repeated encounter sequence. ‘Look—look!—hah!’ written with the first graph for ‘look!’ (顧鑒咦) and the same phrase written with its witness variant (顧鑑咦) are graph variants; ‘drawn look’ (抽顧) is the later shortened form. ‘Reflect’ is retained only as an alternate lexical possibility for ‘look!’ (鑒); the explicit narratives foreground Yunmen saying the word while looking at the recorded questioner, so ‘look!’ is primary. Later aggressive metaphors applied to the sequence are recorded as later comments, not its definition. Frozen-corpus concordance: 29 exact hits in 21 storage files representing 20 independent works.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The expression names Yunmen’s sequence: he looks toward the interlocutor, says “Look!”, and cuts off the attempted answer with “Hah!”
EvidenceBody: Yunmen’s own record describes the interaction: he sometimes looked toward the recorded questioner and said “Look!”; when the questioner prepared to answer, Yunmen said “Hah!” The monasteries consequently named Yunmen by this look-and-two-utterance sequence. A collected transmission states the same sequence and adds that Deshan Yuanming later removed the initial look and called the shortened form “drawn look.” Later texts use the compact phrase as a named case, ask how it operates at face-to-face meeting, and place it alongside Yunmen’s other characteristic responses. The punctuation and speaker sequence matter: this is a recorded look and two utterances, not an abstract three-word maxim.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: For 顧鑒咦, the stored cases establish this term-specific deployment: Literally, ‘look back / look!’ (顧), ‘look, inspect, or reflect!’ (鑒), and the exclamation ‘hah!’ (咦).
